title: Knowing you don't know
hook: to know that you don't know is best (Tao Te Ching 71)

segments.voice: Yesterday, coarse cloth: the sage in a plain coat with jade held inside. Your line was jade inside. Did one good thing stay quiet? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

A meeting. Someone asks a question across the table, and every head turns your way. You half know the answer. Maybe a third. There can be a small, fast pressure to fill the silence with something that sounds right. Three short words would end it honestly, and in a room full of waiting faces, they can be hard to say. Chapter seventy-one of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it's built around those words.
screen: `A QUESTION ACROSS THE TABLE.` → `THE PRESSURE TO SOUND RIGHT.` → `THREE HARD WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. To know that you don't know is highest. Not to know, and to think you know, is a sickness. That's the whole first move: two kinds of not knowing. One is aware of itself. The other is wearing a costume. Second, the turn. The chapter keeps playing with that word sickness. Only when you treat the sickness as a sickness, it says, are you free of it. The sage isn't sick, because the sage sees the sickness for what it is. In other words, nobody is immune to pretending to know. The sage's health is just catching it. Third, a neighbor. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom, and came away thinking he had one small edge on them: they thought they knew what they didn't, and he didn't think he knew. Two thinkers, far apart, landing on the same quiet point. Neither is borrowing from the other; they just arrive at the same door. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. I don't know is not the end of a conversation. It's where a real one starts. It lets the other person teach you. It keeps a guess from hardening into a fact that others then build on. And it's a relief: you put down the work of seeming. Chapter seventy-one doesn't praise ignorance. It praises knowing where your knowing stops.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF NOT KNOWING.` · `CALL THE SICKNESS A SICKNESS.` · `SOCRATES LANDS THERE TOO.` · `WHERE A REAL CONVERSATION STARTS.` · then, large: `KNOWING YOU DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one not-knowing. Sit and let the breath settle. Then bring to mind something you've been acting as if you understand: a topic, a person, a decision, maybe something about yourself. Let it come clearly. Now, silently, say to it: I don't know. Notice what happens in the body when you say it. Some tightness may let go. Some may grip harder. Either is fine to notice. Stay with the open space those words leave. The bell holds the time.
Knowing you don't know. Chapter seventy-one: to know that you don't know is highest; to think you know when you don't is a sickness. Today's word.
Your line: I don't know. Say it out loud once today when it's true, and then ask the question that comes next. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-one as a check on false confidence: being aware of the limits of what you know is counted the healthiest kind of knowing.

pairs: thinking you know when you don't

myth: chapter seventy-one praises not knowing anything
it praises knowing that you don't know: seeing where your knowing stops.
the chapter says the sage is free of the sickness by seeing it as a sickness
the sage isn't immune; the sage recognizes it.
in Plato's Apology, Socrates says his edge was not thinking he knew what he didn't
the people he questioned thought they knew; he didn't think so.

fork.setup: every head at the table turns to you. you half know the answer. what does chapter seventy-one count highest?
options: answer confidently and fix it later.
know that you don't know, and say so.
fork.reveal: to know that you don't know is highest. thinking you know when you don't is what the chapter calls a sickness.

original.note: Chinese: to know not-knowing, the opening of chapter seventy-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowing you don't know is just humility.
what it means: two kinds of not knowing, one aware of itself and one pretending; only the first is healthy.
what a scholar hears: the chapter turns on the word bìng, sickness, repeated until seeing the sickness as sickness becomes the cure.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 71 (to know not-knowing is highest; not knowing yet thinking you know is a sickness; the sage treats the sickness as sickness)
Plato, Apology 21d (Socrates on not thinking he knows what he does not know)

notes: Chapter 71 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording. The first line 知不知上 is read here as 'to know that you don't know is highest'; some translators read 'to know, yet think you do not know'. Confirm the reading.
Plato's Apology is paraphrased (no public-domain translation quoted). Reference 21d given from memory; confirm.
The Socrates parallel is presented as a neighbor, with no claim of influence either way.
Trapdoor: 病 (bìng) as the repeated word in chapter 71; confirm.
Original 知不知 (zhī bù zhī) rendered 'JUR boo JUR'. Confirm.

Editor: cut the unsourced claim that chapter 71 is 'one of the shortest in the book' and the superlative 'hardest three in the room'; the hook no longer tells the listener what they feel in the chest.
